text:
[LSTR.2.1] `len(s)` returns the number of Unicode codepoints
in `s`, as `Int`. Not the byte count, not the grapheme-cluster
count, not the UTF-16 code-unit count. So `café` with a precomposed `é`
(U+00E9) has length 4, and a waving-hand emoji followed by a skin-tone
modifier (U+1F44B U+1F3FD) has length 2, though it renders as one grapheme.

idris.name: lstr_2_1__len
idris.note: `len(s)`: the number of codepoints in the text, as an Int -- not the byte count, not the grapheme-cluster count, not the UTF-16 code-unit count, none of which a text of codepoints has.

idris.name: lstr_2_1__len_counts_codepoints
idris.note: The clause's two examples, executed: `café` is 4 and the waving hand with a skin-tone modifier is 2.

idris.name: lstr_2_1__len_is_total_on_texts
idris.note: `len` of a String is the codepoint count, an Int, for every text. The second conjunct, `len` of `null` a trap, is [IRET.9.6]'s first arm: the clause says nothing of a null receiver.

idris.name: lstr_2_1__len_of
idris.note: `len(<String>)` over its evaluated operand: of a String the codepoint count; of `null` a trap, [IRET.9.6]'s first arm; of a fault the fault. Of a value of any other kind a trap here and not DS: the compiler types `len` by its argument, and a `Json` value's `len` is `lexp_6_1__len`'s. Partial because the null and the other kinds are outside what the clause states.
